Issued at 430 AM CDT Sat Aug 1 2026

Anticyclonic northwest flow lies over the Northern Plains early
this morning, with a traditional ridge axis from the Great Salt
Lake to along the Alberta/Saskatchewan border and an east-
northeast pointing axis from southern North Dakota to Lake 
Superior. There is a 700 mb shortwave traversing southern 
Saskatchewan underneath the broad upper ridge, with low level 
jet induced warm air advection in southeast Saskatchewan and 
southwest Manitoba. This has initiated a small cluster of 
showers and thunderstorms that has crossed into far north 
central North Dakota as of 4 AM CDT. Confidence on maintenance 
of this convection remains low, as forcing is forecast to weaken
and downstream MUCAPE is analyzed to be only 100-200 J/kg. 
After this activity dissipates or departs to the east, quiet 
weather is expected to prevail through the rest of the day, with
increasing southerly return flow over central North Dakota 
between a downstream surface ridge and upstream lee troughing. 
Temperatures are projected to reach around 100 degrees in 
southwest parts of the state this afternoon, with 90s northwest 
and central and mid to upper 80s from the Turtle Mountains 
through the James River Valley. Dewpoints in the mid 40 to mid 
50s should keep heat indices below 100 in southwest North Dakota
this afternoon, and the probability of widespread temperatures 
at or above 100 is not high enough to issue a Heat Advisory. But
it will still be a very hot day, and precautions should still 
be taken to avoid over-exposure to the heat. Very few, if any 
clouds are expected today, but smoke aloft could produce a hazy 
sky.

From this evening into Sunday morning, the main upper ridge 
axis will be tilted in a positive direction as a well-advertised
upper low crosses the Canadian Rockies. An overnight southerly 
breeze around 10 to 15 mph should keep low temperatures in the 
60s to lower 70s. Southerly winds will then strengthen over 
central North Dakota by Sunday afternoon, and may approach 
advisory criteria of sustained winds near 30 mph and gusts near 
45 mph. This will take place ahead of a cold front being driven 
in by the Canadian low. By mid afternoon, the cold front is 
projected to be roughly located from the Turtle Mountains to 
Standing Rock Reservation. High temperatures along the frontal 
interface in the southern half of the state could easily reach 
100 degrees, and few locations could approach 105 on account of 
compressional heating. Moisture return in the downstream 
southerly flow could bring mid 50s to mid 60s dewpoints back 
into central North Dakota, which introduces a higher probability
of heat indices reaching 100 Sunday afternoon. The latest NBM 
guidance highlights this in a corridor from Bismarck through 
eastern Grant and western Sioux Counties, and the maximum wet-
bulb globe temperature risk also reaches the Extreme category in
this area. Elsewhere on Sunday, expecting highs in the 90s 
surrounding the aforementioned corridor, with mid to upper 80s 
in both the far northwest and southern James River Valley. Winds
behind the cold front are not projected to be overly strong, 
but could still gust to near 30 mph in far western North Dakota 
Sunday afternoon. With humidity falling into the 15 to 25 
percent range across the western half of the state, and perhaps 
closer to 10 percent in the far southwest, at least near-
critical fire weather conditions are expected. There are 
currently two separate areas with the highest probabilities for 
meeting Red Flag Warning criteria on Sunday: one across Golden 
Valley, Slope, and Bowman Counties and another in eastern Sioux,
western Emmons, and southern Burleigh Counties. But these 
probabilities are still not quite high enough for a Fire Weather
Watch, and the disjointed areas of highest probabilities lowers
confidence in spatial coverage. Further complicating matters is
that each of the 2 areas of concern occur at different times of
day (early afternoon far southwest and mid to late afternoon 
south central). A final note about Sunday is that HRRR/RAP 
guidance projects a significant increase in near-surface smoke 
concentrations with the arrival of the cold front, which is a 
regime the modeling has proven to perform well in.

The cold front is forecast to stall from northeast to south 
central North Dakota Sunday evening as its parent cyclone begins
to occlude over central Saskatchewan. It is very doubtful that 
the cold front will be able to initiate any convection on its 
own prior to sunset Sunday evening, with strong capping in place
and stronger mid/upper level ascent lagging behind. Heading 
into Sunday night though, shortwave energy embedded in southwest
flow aloft could begin traversing the region as the rate of mid
level height falls increases, and northeastward moisture 
transport from the nocturnal low level jet is also forecast to 
strengthen. This increases probabilities for elevated convection
